title: The List module in practice
body: `List` is the workhorse of everyday OCaml. Learn the families: transform (`map`, `mapi`, `filter_map`, `concat_map`), summarise (`fold_left`, `exists`, `for_all`, `length`), search (`find_opt`, `assoc_opt`, `mem`), reorder (`sort`, `rev`, `sort_uniq`) and split or join (`partition`, `combine`, `split`, `flatten`).

Pick the function that states your intent. `filter_map` replaces a filter followed by a map when the mapping can fail, and `concat_map` replaces map followed by flatten. A clear combinator is easier to read and to optimise than a hand-written recursion.

Remember cost. `List.nth` and `@` walk the list, so using them in a loop makes it quadratic. If you index often, convert to an array once. Many `List` functions are not tail-recursive on very long lists in older compilers, so check the manual if you process millions of elements.
challenge: Given words, use List.filter_map to keep the lengths of words longer than 3 characters, then print their sum.
solution:
let () =
  let words = ["a"; "tree"; "is"; "green"] in
  let lens = List.filter_map (fun w -> let n = String.length w in if n > 3 then Some n else None) words in
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (List.fold_left ( + ) 0 lens)
question: Which function replaces a filter followed by a map when the mapping can fail?
reasoning: filter_map applies a function returning an option and keeps only the Some results, doing both steps in one pass.

title: Arrays, strings and bytes
body: An `array` has a fixed length, constant-time indexing and in-place update with `a.(i) <- v`. Create one with `Array.make`, `Array.init` or a literal `[| 1; 2; 3 |]`. Index out of range raises `Invalid_argument`, which the compiler cannot catch in advance.

`string` is immutable text. Operations like `String.sub`, `String.split_on_char` and `String.concat` return new strings. When you need to build or change text efficiently, use `Bytes` (mutable) or `Buffer` (growable), and convert at the end with `Bytes.to_string` or `Buffer.contents`.

Prefer `Buffer` for appending in a loop, because repeated `^` copies the whole string every time and becomes quadratic. Treat strings as byte sequences, so `String.length` counts bytes, not Unicode characters.
challenge: Reverse the string "stressed" by copying its characters into Bytes in reverse order, then print the result.
question: Why use Buffer instead of repeated `^` when building a long string in a loop?
correct: Each ^ copies the whole string, so a loop becomes quadratic; Buffer appends in amortised constant time
wrong: Because ^ only works for two characters
reasoning: Strings are immutable, so each concatenation allocates a new copy; a Buffer grows in place and copies once at the end.

title: Hashtbl for mutable lookup tables
body: `Hashtbl` is a mutable hash table: `Hashtbl.create 16`, `add`/`replace`, `find_opt`, `mem` and `remove`. Lookup and update are on average constant time, which is what you want for counting, caching and memoisation.

Know the difference between `add` and `replace`. `add` hides an older binding for the same key but keeps it underneath, so `find_all` returns every binding, while `replace` overwrites. Most code wants `replace`, and `find_opt` instead of the exception-raising `find`.

Iteration order is unspecified, so sort the keys before printing. The default `Hashtbl.hash` is structural and only looks at a bounded amount of a value; for keys with custom equality, use the functor `Hashtbl.Make` with your own `equal` and `hash`.
challenge: Memoise a slow Fibonacci with a Hashtbl and print fib 40.
solution:
let memo = Hashtbl.create 64

let rec fib n =
  if n < 2 then n
  else match Hashtbl.find_opt memo n with
    | Some v -> v
    | None -> let v = fib (n - 1) + fib (n - 2) in Hashtbl.replace memo n v; v

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (fib 40)
question: Why sort the keys before printing a Hashtbl's contents?
correct: Iteration order is unspecified, so output would otherwise vary
wrong: Hashtbl stores keys in sorted order already
reasoning: Hash tables do not guarantee any traversal order, so deterministic output needs an explicit sort.

title: Persistent Map and Set
body: `Map.Make` and `Set.Make` are functors: you give them a module with a type `t` and a `compare` function, and you get a persistent (immutable) balanced tree. `module IntMap = Map.Make (Int)` yields maps with int keys.

Operations return new maps and leave the old one intact, so you can keep previous versions cheaply. Lookup, insert and remove are logarithmic. Iteration with `fold` or `bindings` is in sorted key order, which makes the output deterministic.

Use `Map` when you need ordered keys, sharing or immutability, and `Hashtbl` when you want mutable constant-time updates. A common mistake is expecting a `Map` operation to modify its argument; remember to bind the result.
challenge: Build a Map from string to int counting how many times each letter appears in "banana" (use SMap.update) and print it in key order.
question: What happens to the original map after `SMap.add "c" 3 m1`?
correct: It is unchanged; add returns a new map that shares structure with it
wrong: It gains the new binding in place
reasoning: Map is a persistent data structure, so every update produces a new value while old versions stay valid.

title: Seq: lazy sequences
body: A `Seq.t` is a lazy, possibly infinite sequence: a function that produces the next element only when asked. This lets you describe `naturals`, `primes` or a file's lines without building a whole list in memory.

Combinators such as `Seq.map`, `Seq.filter`, `Seq.take` and `Seq.fold_left` mirror the `List` functions but compute on demand. Nothing runs until a consumer like `fold_left`, `iter` or `List.of_seq` forces it, so you must bound an infinite sequence with `take` before collecting it.

Sequences are ephemeral by default: an effectful source may produce different results if you traverse it twice. Use `Seq.memoize` when you need to traverse a costly sequence more than once, and prefer a list when the data is small and reused.
challenge: Use Seq.unfold to produce the first 8 powers of two and print them.
question: When does a Seq pipeline actually compute elements?
correct: When a consumer such as fold_left, iter or List.of_seq demands them
wrong: As soon as each combinator is applied
reasoning: Seq values are functions producing the next element on demand, so combinators only build the plan.

title: Formatting text: sprintf, Format and custom printers
body: `Printf.sprintf` returns a string instead of printing, so it is the standard way to build messages. The format string is typed, which is why `sprintf "%d" "x"` is a compile error. Padding and precision work as in C: `%5d`, `%-5s`, `%05.1f`.

The `Format` module adds pretty-printing: boxes, break hints and automatic line breaking at a margin. A printer for your type has the shape `Format.formatter -> t -> unit`, and you use it with `%a`, such as `Format.asprintf "%a" pp_point p`.

Write a `pp` function for every public type. Doing so gives toplevel printers, test failure messages and logging a single readable place, and later lessons on `ppx_deriving`/`ppx_jane` generate this boilerplate for you.
challenge: Write `pp_list pp_elt` that prints a list as `[a; b; c]` using Format.pp_print_list with a "; " separator, and print `[1; 2; 3]` with it.
question: What is the shape of a Format printer for type t?
reasoning: %a takes a function that writes to a formatter and then the value to print, so printers compose.
